issues.legal_issue: A co-mortgagor who redeems a joint mortgage for less than the debt then due may recover from the other co-mortgagors only their proportionate shares of the amount actually paid.
material_facts: The mortgage had been executed jointly, and the redeeming co-mortgagor redeemed it for his own benefit after the joint family had ceased to exist.
He paid Rs. 5,800 to redeem the mortgage, although Rs. 11,200 was due under its terms.
He claimed that the other co-mortgagors should contribute according to the larger amount due, rather than the amount he had actually paid.
The Transfer of Property Act did not apply in the relevant jurisdiction, so the dispute was governed by principles of equity, justice and good conscience.
issues.conclusion: The redeeming co-mortgagor could recover only the other co-mortgagors’ proportionate shares of the amount actually paid to redeem the mortgage, not shares calculated on the full amount that had been due.
issues.legal_principle: Subrogation is an equitable doctrine that protects a redeeming co-mortgagor’s right to reimbursement or contribution; it does not permit recovery from the other co-mortgagors beyond their shares of the amount actually and properly paid. The Court relied on Hodgson v. Shaw, Digambar Das v. Harendra Narayan Panday and Suryanarayana v. Sriramulu. It applied general principles of equity, justice and good conscience because the Transfer of Property Act did not apply; it therefore did not decide whether sections 92 or 95 of that Act altered the equitable rule, and it steered clear of the old sections 74 and 75.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns contribution after a co-mortgagor redeems a joint mortgage under equitable principles, and the redemption payment was below the amount due but the claim exceeds the others’ shares of that payment, the contribution is limited to their shares of the amount paid.

issues.legal_issue: A deed recording redemption and payment does not establish an assignment of the mortgage without words assigning the security.
material_facts: The redeeming co-mortgagor relied on a registered deed of redemption as an assignment of the mortgage.
The deed contained no words assigning the security, and the mortgage deed bore an endorsement recording payment; the mortgagee stated that the property had been released from the mortgage.
issues.conclusion: The deed did not assign the mortgage to the redeeming co-mortgagor.
issues.legal_principle: An assertion that a person is to be the owner of the amount due from mortgaged property is different from an assignment of the mortgage security. The absence of assignment language, together with an endorsement acknowledging payment and a statement releasing the property, indicated redemption rather than assignment.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns an alleged mortgage assignment and the registered redemption deed lacks assignment words, payment is endorsed on the mortgage, and the mortgagee released the property, an assignment is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for possession and partition may be joined with a claim for redemption in the same suit when no limitation issue prevents that course.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession and partition of their shares in property after a co-sharer had redeemed a mortgage.
The objection that the suit was not maintainable without a separate redemption suit was raised before the High Court.
No question of limitation was involved.
issues.conclusion: The claims for redemption, possession and partition could be joined in the same suit, so the maintainability objection failed.
issues.legal_principle: Where no question of limitation is involved, a claim for redemption may be joined with a claim for possession and partition in the same suit.
